response.passage: Gravity is a fundamental force of attraction that exists between every pair of objects in the universe, regardless of their size. Whether it is a massive planet or a small pen, every object exerts a gravitational pull on others. When an object falls towards the Earth, it experiences free fall. In a perfect vacuum where air resistance is absent, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration regardless of their mass. This happens because the Earth pulls on every object with a force proportional to its mass, but the object's inertia resists this motion in exactly the same proportion. Furthermore, gravity does not stop at the edge of our atmosphere; it extends infinitely into space, weakening only as distance increases. When you submerge an object in water, it may feel lighter due to the upward buoyant force, but its actual mass remains completely unchanged. This buoyant force is determined by the volume of water displaced by the object, not by the object's own weight. Finally, pressure is defined as force applied over a specific area. A sharp nail exerts high pressure because its force is concentrated on a tiny surface area, whereas a flat board spreads the same force over a large area, resulting in much lower pressure.
response.summary: Gravity is a universal force acting on all objects, and its effects like free fall and pressure depend on physical laws rather than just an object's weight. Submerging an object in water creates a buoyant force that makes it feel lighter, even though its mass stays the same.
